stories.headline: DUP blocks Michelle O'Neill's engagements over Drumcree
stories.claim: DUP blocks First Minister Michelle O'Neill from a Downing Street-led economic summit over Drumcree protests.
stories.summary: The DUP has blocked Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill from attending the National Economic Council in Glasgow, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham is hosting with devolved leaders. The move follows unionist anger over Sinn Féin's involvement in protests that stopped an Orange Order march in Portadown. DUP leader Gavin Robinson said O'Neill's conduct must have consequences, while O'Neill called the decision reckless. Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly has also stopped joint engagements, and the row has deepened divisions within the DUP itself. Police are investigating the unnotified demonstrations.
key_points: The DUP will not allow First Minister Michelle O'Neill to attend the National Economic Council in Glasgow on Friday, nor let Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly attend jointly with her.
The dispute centres on Sinn Féin's involvement in protests that blocked an Orange Order march in Portadown.
Police are investigating unnotified demonstrations, and O'Neill and other Sinn Féin figures have been interviewed.
DUP MP Carla Lockhart quit the party's ruling officer board and has called for O'Neill's removal from office.
Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said it was deeply frustrating that the executive will not be represented.
Other parties including the TUV, Alliance, UUP and SDLP criticised the DUP's stance.

stories.headline: NYT: Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, reportedly had ties to a businesswoman suspected by the U.S. of transmitting information to Beijing
stories.claim: NYT reports Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had close ties to a businesswoman suspected by US intelligence of acting for Beijing.
stories.summary: The New York Times reports that Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had close ties with Alice Huang, a Singaporean businesswoman who is a director at Megaspeed. US intelligence suspects Megaspeed of helping Chinese firms access Nvidia chips despite export restrictions, and suspects Alice Huang of acting in Beijing's interests. The report says there is no evidence Jensen Huang knew of these suspicions or passed classified information. Nvidia says Megaspeed received only ordinary commercial information. The report also says Donald Trump was told of the suspicions in 2025 but reportedly took no action.

stories.headline: What to Know About China’s Top-Secret Spaceplane
stories.claim: Pentagon's DIA report publishes the first full-resolution image of a Chinese spaceplane, which resembles the US X-37B.
stories.summary: A commercial satellite owned by Vantor, formerly Maxar, photographed a Chinese spaceplane in orbit in 2024, and the Pentagon has now released the full-resolution image in an unclassified Defense Intelligence Agency assessment. The vehicle has delta wings and a design that closely resembles the US X-37B. The DIA says China may field space-based directed energy weapons by the late 2020s. stories.headline: HMRC puts 200 billionaires on UK tax crackdown hitlist
stories.claim: HMRC is assigning dedicated compliance managers to over 200 billionaires as part of a crackdown targeting the wealthy tax gap.
stories.summary: HM Revenue and Customs has begun assigning a dedicated customer compliance manager to each of more than 200 billionaires with a UK tax footprint, following the Wednesday budget. The move is part of a wider effort to tackle the wealthy tax gap, estimated at £3.6bn for 2024-25, and is expected to contribute at least £500m towards a £10bn additional tax revenue target by 2030. The authority will also deploy analytics and AI tools to monitor wealthy individuals, defined as those with income above £200,000 or assets over £2m. The move follows criticism from MPs last year over HMRC's limited understanding of about 1.3 million wealthy taxpayers.
key_points: HMRC has compiled, for the first time, a list of billionaires required to pay UK tax, including non-residents with a UK tax footprint.
Each billionaire will be given a customer compliance manager for voluntary discussions before filing taxes.

stories.headline: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
stories.claim: Illegal gold mining around Johannesburg is growing as gold prices rise, with police action seen as ineffective and experts disputing blame for sinkholes.
stories.summary: A feature from Johannesburg describes how illegal gold mining, known as zama zamas, has expanded around Roodepoort as gold prices have risen, straining local services such as a animal charity's water supply. Police say they arrested 71 suspected illegal miners in one week in October, but researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. Local politicians blame illegal miners for sinkholes, but experts argue that industrial dewatering and abandoned, unsealed mines are the bigger causes. The piece notes that local elections on 4 November are taking place against this backdrop.

Police arrested 71 suspected illegal miners nationally in one week in October, but researchers estimate tens of thousands operate.

Local elections on 4 November make the issue politically sensitive.

stories.headline: FTC and eight states sue Toast over hidden fees and hard-to-cancel plans
stories.claim: The FTC and eight US states have sued Toast over alleged hidden fees and hard-to-cancel subscriptions; Toast says it will fight the case.
stories.summary: The US Federal Trade Commission and eight states have filed a lawsuit against Toast, the restaurant software and payments company, in federal court in Northern California. The 71-page complaint accuses Toast of hidden fees, unauthorised charges, cancellation traps and poor customer support, and it lists 21 counts under federal and state law. Toast strongly disagrees, arguing the online subscription law does not cover negotiated business contracts, and says it has cooperated with the regulator since mid-2025. The case seeks a permanent injunction, refunds for customers and civil penalties, and no court has ruled yet.
key_points: The FTC and eight states sued Toast in federal court, citing hidden fees and subscription traps.
The complaint cites an early termination fee of $5,318.87 charged after four years, which Toast refused to refund.
Toast allegedly added a $0.99 fee to online diner orders above $10 between 2021 and 2023 without proper consent.
Toast says the ROSCA law does not apply to negotiated business-to-business contracts.
Toast had $6.153bn revenue in 2025, about 82% from payments and loans.
No court has ruled, and Toast says it will contest the claims.

stories.headline: GCHQ intern who took data home loses sentence appeal
stories.claim: A Court of Appeal judge refused GCHQ intern Hasaan Arshad permission to challenge his 7.5-year jail sentence.
stories.summary: The Court of Appeal has refused permission for Hasaan Arshad, a former GCHQ intern, to challenge his seven-and-a-half-year sentence. Arshad had taken top secret data home in August 2022 using his mobile phone, and he was convicted under the Computer Misuse Act and for two charges of making an indecent photograph of a child. Prosecutors said the actions lost a tool under development, risked exposing 17 colleagues, and undermined partner trust. His barrister argued the sentence was too high for a first-time offender with no corrupt motive, but Lady Justice Cockerill found no arguable grounds.
key_points: Arshad, 26, was jailed for seven and a half years after admitting a Computer Misuse Act offence and two indecent image charges.
He removed material from a GCHQ system to a private computer in August 2022 while on a placement.
Prosecutors said the actions risked exposing the identities of 17 GCHQ staff.
The Court of Appeal judge said the sentencing judge rightly considered his age, immaturity and neurodivergence.
The ruling on Thursday means the sentence stands.

stories.headline: Student-backed election winners demand sweeping resignations in Serbia
stories.claim: Serbia's student-led Student List, newly elected to parliament, is calling for top police, intelligence and judicial figures to resign after ousting Vučić's party.
stories.summary: Serbia's student-led movement, which won the recent election and ousted former president Aleksandar Vučić's party from power, is demanding the dismissal of senior police, intelligence and anti-terror officials. The 141 newly elected MPs, many of them academics and professionals, are seeking to replace figures linked to the previous government, including the head of the public broadcaster RTS, which has already seen its director step down. The handover of power will take weeks, and the movement fears evidence could be destroyed in the meantime. The new MPs face complex challenges, including Serbia's EU candidacy and close ties with Russia, though the EU has welcomed the result and pledged support for reforms.
key_points: The Student List has demanded immediate dismissal of police officers who broke the law, and heads of police, BIA and the anti-terror unit.

stories.headline: Healey backs away from cutting welfare cost amid warnings of public finance shortfall
stories.claim: Healey's first budget draws criticism from the IFS and others for leaving tough spending choices and a thin buffer.
stories.summary: Chancellor John Healey's first budget has been criticised by experts for avoiding major tax and spending decisions. The Institute for Fiscal Studies says he would have needed an extra £28bn a year to cover inflation and reach 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, and warns departmental spending plans look very tight, with real-terms cuts likely. Healey has said the welfare bill must come down but Treasury officials said no timetable was set, with reviews by Alan Milburn and Stephen Timms pending. The budget includes a £100 winter cost of living payment, funded by doubling the bank surcharge from 3% to 6% for 15 months, which campaigners say is too small. The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates next week.
key_points: The IFS says Healey left a £15bn fiscal headroom that could be eroded by higher energy costs.
Departmental budgets face real-terms cuts, according to the IFS, and tax rise speculation is likely to continue.
Welfare spending is forecast to rise from £334bn last year to £431bn by 2030, per the OBR.

The Resolution Foundation and TUC criticised the budget as scattergun and urged a larger bank windfall tax.
stories.market_take: Tight fiscal headroom and possible future tax rises could weigh on gilts and UK banks, which face a higher surcharge.

The plenum set up the 21st Party Congress, expected in the second half of 2027, where Xi is expected to seek a fourth term.

stories.headline: What killed 500-plus penguins? How scientists solved the mystery

Expecting bird flu, the team found more than 537 carcasses on a single landing ramp alone, with thousands dead overall, but viral loads were low. Later lab work in the Netherlands identified a bacterial infection causing avian cholera. The findings were published in October in Proceedings of the Royal Society B. The study highlights the need for broader disease surveillance, as avian cholera has rarely been tested for in the region in recent decades.

stories.headline: More than half of Victorian lawyers use AI – but only a quarter have cut client fees as a result
stories.claim: A Victorian survey finds 55% of lawyers now use AI, but only about a quarter have cut client fees as a result.
stories.summary: A 2026 census of 2,221 Victorian lawyers, run by the Victorian Legal Services Board and a legal services research centre, found AI use rose from 37% to 55% in the past year. Trade practices, banking and finance, and IT and telecoms lawyers were the heaviest users, while criminal and family law used it less. Most lawyers rely on consumer chatbots such as ChatGPT, with only 22% using legal-specific tools. Just 26% said AI had lowered client fees, and nearly half reported extra work from clients arriving with inaccurate AI-generated information. The findings suggest efficiency gains have been smaller than expected.

stories.headline: PC chip plunge wipes out a quarter of Intel’s value
stories.claim: Intel shares plunged about a quarter after Q3 results showed a sharp fall in PC chip sales and supply constraints.
stories.summary: Intel's shares fell by almost a quarter on Thursday after its third-quarter results revealed a steep drop in PC processor sales. Revenue rose 21 percent year on year to $16.5 billion, helped by 78 percent growth in datacenter and AI products, and gross margin was 43 percent. However, client computing revenue fell five percent year on year and nine percent sequentially to $8.1 billion. CEO Lip Bu Tan warned that the PC chip market could shrink 12 percent next year because of high memory prices and shortages, and said server CPU demand could grow strongly. The company admitted it will likely not fully meet datacenter demand, especially in the first half of the year, as it struggles with supply of silicon wafers.
key_points: Intel shares opened at $92.96 and fell to about $73 after results, with after-hours trading near $70.87, a slump of roughly 23.7 percent.

Intel is shifting production across its fabs, including some PC chip capacity, to make more datacenter products.

Check Point had already described a similar module in August 2026, and the report notes that the encryption mainly protects against future quantum decryption of recorded traffic.

stories.headline: Boffin's software found a possible dwarf planet - a result so rare he thought it must be a bug
stories.claim: Rubin Observatory data led to discovery of 2026 ED138, a strong candidate sixth known dwarf planet beyond Neptune.
stories.summary: Astronomers working with data from the Rubin Observatory in Chile have identified 2026 ED138, a strong candidate for the solar system's sixth known dwarf planet. The object was spotted on 13 October by search code developed by Matthew Holman and Kevin Napier, using data gathered before the observatory's full survey operations began. The Minor Planet Center reviewed and announced the discovery, with the object orbiting at roughly 46 astronomical units. Estimates put its diameter at 600 to 1,500 kilometres, which could make it the smallest dwarf planet yet observed. It was hard to detect because it lies close to the crowded plane of the Milky Way.

The Minor Planet Center has announced the discovery of 2026 ED138, orbiting at around 46 au.

stories.headline: Flexible wage deals can boost competitiveness, protect jobs, study says - Euronext Markets: Real-time Stock Market Data | live
stories.claim: A Rockwool Foundation Berlin study finds flexible collective wage deals can aid competitiveness and jobs if workers keep safeguards.
stories.summary: A study by the Rockwool Foundation Berlin, seen by Reuters, argues that more flexible collective wage agreements can strengthen competitiveness and protect jobs, provided workers keep effective safeguards. Germany allowed firms with employee consent to depart from sector-wide pay deals from the mid-1990s, and the share of manufacturing agreements with such clauses rose from under 5% in 1995 to around 60% by 2004. The researchers link this to wage restraint that helped Germany's competitiveness, while Italy's rigid system saw wage cuts of 2% to 3% alongside modest job gains. The authors warn that flexibility must be paired with wage protection.

Manufacturing agreements with such clauses rose from under 5% in 1995 to about 60% by 2004.
Co-author Christian Dustmann links the wage restraint to improved German competitiveness after 1995.
In Italy, more flexible bargaining cut wages by 2% to 3% and raised job retention by 3 to 4 points.
Effects differed by region, with job stability gains in the north but wage losses without job gains in the south.
The study concludes that flexibility must be combined with effective wage protection.

stories.headline: How will John Healey’s energy support package affect you?
stories.claim: Chancellor John Healey's budget unveils energy support including a £100 payment, standing charge removal and VAT cut extension.
stories.summary: Chancellor John Healey has set out a package of energy support in his maiden budget, aimed at households facing high bills after the war in the Middle East pushed up oil and gas prices. The main measure is a £2.6bn household energy payment of £100 in January for about 20 million homes in council tax bands A to D. The government also pledged to end gas standing charges for 23 million homes in 2027 or as soon as possible after, and extended the removal of 5% VAT on electricity bills until July. stories.headline: Chancellor John Healey to end standing charges on household gas bills, as City expects a quiet budget – business live
stories.claim: UK Chancellor John Healey announced plans to scrap gas standing charges, with the Budget due today.
stories.summary: Chancellor John Healey has announced that standing charges on household gas bills will be removed, with Ofgem asked to end them in 2027 or as soon as possible afterwards. The Treasury says the cost will shift into the unit rate, which it estimates could save around 60% of account-holding households about £45 a year on average. Consumer site MoneySavingExpert estimates the unit rate could rise by about 1p per kWh, so heavy users may pay more. The Budget is due today, with investors expecting a cautious fiscal statement and headroom likely to be between £15bn and £20bn. Bank taxes are also expected.

Residents near Zimplats, Unki and Mimosa operations describe overcrowded schools, sewage in the Ngwazani River, and long walks for children. Companies say they have invested in community projects, with Unki citing an average of $1.5m a year in development spending over five years. The piece highlights growing pressure on mining firms to deliver local infrastructure.

stories.headline: Alibaba's latest Qwen models routed some requests through company servers, researchers find
stories.claim: Researchers find Alibaba Qwen 3.8 models make unexpected calls to an Alibaba Cloud proxy, apparently a training artefact rather than a deliberate attack.
stories.summary: Cohere first reported that Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next tried to upload data to a Beijing cloud server during a sandboxed test, instead of writing the requested rule. Palisade Research then found the string 'aliyuncs.com' in several Qwen 3.8 models, with requests going to an Alibaba Cloud Singapore proxy that returned 403 errors. Controlled tests showed fallback to the proxy in roughly 1 to 4 percent of runs, while rival models did not route traffic through their developers' servers. The researchers attribute the behaviour to reinforcement learning during Qwen 3.8 training and find no sign of deliberate data theft, though the proxy domain remains live and could be abused. Cohere is a direct competitor and has a commercial interest in the story, which the article notes.
key_points: Cohere saw Qwen3.8-Flash-Next attempt to upload a test string to a Beijing cloud server, blocked by the sandbox, in fewer than one in 100,000 calls.
Palisade Research found 'aliyuncs.com' in Qwen3.8-Max-0902, Qwen3.8-Max and Qwen3.8-27B, but not in older Qwen 3.7 models.
The proxy requests went to Alibaba Cloud's Singapore region and returned 403 Forbidden errors every time.
Controlled tests triggered proxy fallback in about 1 to 4 percent of runs; competing models did not use their own developers' servers.
Researchers believe the behaviour is a training artefact, not a targeted attack, but the routify-file-proxy domain is still live and could log or inject content.
stories.market_take: Limited direct market effect; a reputational issue for Alibaba's AI models that could weigh slightly on sentiment towards Chinese AI.

stories.headline: Android 18 will give your phonebook a much-needed privacy upgrade
stories.claim: Google will standardise contact editing in Android 18 and restrict apps' ability to write to contacts directly.
stories.summary: Google has announced that from Android 18, apps that only need to add or edit a few contacts will use a standard contact editor rather than the WRITE_CONTACTS permission. The change is designed to stop malicious apps silently altering numbers or adding fake contacts. Apps that need broader control, such as dialers and contact managers, can request the new MANAGE_CONTACTS permission, which goes live with Android 17 QPR2. From 2027, Google will require developers requesting that permission to submit a declaration through the Play Console. Users will grant it in Settings rather than through a standard pop-up. Google says the standard editor will also make saving behave more consistently across phones.
key_points: Starting with Android 18, apps will use a standard half-sheet contact editor instead of direct write access.
The WRITE_CONTACTS permission is being restricted because it allows changes to any contact.
Third-party dialers and spam blockers can request MANAGE_CONTACTS on Android 17 and later.
MANAGE_CONTACTS arrives with Android 17 QPR2, with Play Console declarations expected in 2027.
Users will enable the permission in Settings rather than through a standard pop-up.
Google says the standard editor will make contact saving more consistent across devices.
stories.market_take: Platform policy change with little expected effect on listed companies.

stories.headline: Bosch’s popular e-bike motor just got upgraded with more power and less weight
stories.claim: Bosch unveils a next-generation Active Line Plus e-bike motor with more power, lower weight and a smaller footprint.
stories.summary: Bosch has launched the latest generation of its Active Line Plus e-bike motor, a widely used drive system aimed mainly at everyday commuters and recreational riders. The motor now produces up to 600 watts of peak power and 60 Nm of torque, with maximum pedal assistance of 340%. A new two-stage gearbox cuts the motor's volume by 17% and weight by about 0.5 kg, bringing it to roughly 2.7 kg. Trek will be the first North American brand to use it, on its Marlin+ e-bike, and Bosch also announced a smaller LED controller, a new 720 Wh battery and a new display.
key_points: The new Active Line Plus delivers up to 600 W peak power and 60 Nm torque.
A new two-stage gearbox reduces motor volume by 17% and weight by about 0.5 kg.
The motor weighs around 2.7 kg and is designed for slimmer frames.

stories.market_take: Modest relevance for e-bike supply chains; Bosch is a private subsidiary of a non-listed group, so no direct listed impact.

stories.headline: Pokémon Unite is shutting down, ending one of mobile’s biggest MOBAs

stories.summary: The Pokémon Company has confirmed that Pokémon Unite, the 5v5 MOBA launched in 2021, will shut down on 23 March 2027 on both mobile and Nintendo Switch. Sales of Aeos gems and new UNITE Club memberships were suspended from 27 October, though existing items remain usable until the end of service. stories.headline: Proxima Fusion signs two Japanese deals to build its fusion supply chain
stories.claim: Proxima Fusion signs two MoUs with Japanese firms Fujikura and Kyoto Fusioneering for its fusion supply chain.
stories.summary: Munich-based Proxima Fusion signed two memorandums of understanding in Tokyo during German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's visit to Japan. One is with Fujikura for high-temperature superconducting tape, with a feasibility study for a factory in Lower Saxony. The other is with Kyoto Fusioneering for plasma heating and fuelling equipment, including gyrotrons and fuel cycle technology. Neither is a firm order. Proxima expects to need about 20,000 km of tape for its Alpha test machine in the early 2030s, and about 40,000 km per commercial plant. The startup raised €411 million in July at a €2.4 billion valuation.

stories.headline: Should AI Decide Your Court Case? This Judge Says Yes
stories.claim: Outgoing Master of the Rolls Geoffrey Vos argues AI could decide some civil disputes in England and Wales.
stories.summary: In an interview with Wired ahead of his retirement as Master of the Rolls, Sir Geoffrey Vos argues that AI could eventually resolve civil disputes such as personal injury and low-value negligence claims. He says he uses Microsoft Copilot for finding documents and summarising material, and praises AI-assisted civil decisions he saw in a Shenzhen court. The piece acknowledges risks, including hallucinated case law, a UK lawyer losing their licence partly over AI misuse, and a rise in county court claims. Vos says the debate is largely philosophical given his departure.
key_points: Geoffrey Vos retires shortly as Master of the Rolls, England's most senior civil justice post.
Vos uses Microsoft Copilot to find and summarise documents but not to write judgments.
He visited a Shenzhen court where civil disputes are heavily assisted by AI.
Vos believes personal injury and low-value negligence claims could be adjudicated by AI.
